idiom_name: PORO screen state plus listener callbacks; observer gem's Observable mixin for change notification
implementation_notes: Ruby ships no binding and no UI toolkit in the default stack, so the presentation model is a plain old Ruby object: attr_accessor/attr_reader for state and derived decisions, ordinary methods for commands, and - when the view must be told about changes - either an explicit callback list or the observer gem's Observable mixin (require 'observer'), which provides add_observer/notify_observers and requires the object to call changed before notifying. That contract is not enforced (the documentation notes the publisher/subscriber contract is not declared), so every mutating method must call changed/notify_observers itself. In Rails, a plain form/state object beats stashing the screen state in controller instance variables; keep it free of view or request types so specs can drive it directly.
code_sketch:
class AlbumPM
  include Observable                      # observer gem (stdlib before Ruby 3.0)
  attr_reader :classical

  def classical=(value)
    @classical = value
    changed                               # Observable only notifies while changed
    notify_observers(self)
  end

  def composer_enabled? = @classical      # decision
  def apply = @data.save                  # command
end
pitfalls: Observable notifies only while the changed flag is set, and notify_observers resets it to false - a forgotten changed call silently drops an update.
Observable keeps observers in a hash with strong references; an observer that is never removed through delete_observer keeps the discarded view alive.
attr_accessor writes do not notify: a direct ivar assignment bypasses the setter that calls changed, so all mutation must go through the notifying writer.
Ruby's GVL makes single assignments atomic but not composite updates: two threads interleaving writer calls can leave the model with a state combination no command produced.
